sum: At a drinking party celebrating the playwright Agathon’s victory, the guests agree to take turns giving speeches in praise of Eros, the god of love. The talk moves from myth and medicine to comedy and tragedy, and then to Socrates’ account of love as a ladder rising from desire for one beautiful person toward beauty itself, before a drunken Alcibiades bursts in and turns the evening upside down.
bg: The Symposium is among Plato’s most literary works, told at several removes as a story someone heard from someone who was there. Its speeches include Aristophanes’ famous myth that humans were once double creatures, split in two, who now search for their other halves.
br: Short enough to read in one or two sittings. Enjoy each speech as a character portrait as well as an argument; the order matters, and each speaker answers or one-ups the last.
la: The dialogue builds through rival speeches toward Socrates’ lofty vision, which he attributes to a wise woman named Diotima, then deliberately undercuts it with Alcibiades’ painful, comic confession of unrequited love for Socrates himself.
cx: The work reflects the customs of elite male Athenian society, including relationships between older men and youths, which shape its account of love. It has been read for centuries as a founding text on desire, and gave us the phrase Platonic love.
th: Desire and lack
We love what we do not yet have, and love itself is a kind of longing.
Beauty and ascent
Love can lead from one body to all beauty and then to ideas.
Philosophy as a way of life
Socrates lives what he argues, which is both admirable and maddening.
fit: A lighter, warmer entry point to Plato that pairs with the romance and the moral philosophy on your list.
mis: The social world of the speeches can feel distant, and the nested framing may confuse at first.
cw: Frank discussion of relationships between men and adolescent boys in ancient Athens.
rq: Which speech comes closest to your own view of love?
Why does Socrates credit his account to Diotima?
What does Alcibiades reveal about Socrates that no one else does?
dq: Is Platonic love a loss or a gain compared with other loves?
Why does Plato end with Alcibiades rather than Socrates?
rel: Plato’s larger account of the soul and the good.

sum: Plato’s version of the speech Socrates gave at his trial in 399 BCE, accused of impiety and corrupting the young. Socrates explains the mission that made him enemies, questioning everyone who claimed to be wise, refuses to beg for mercy or bring his weeping children into court, and faces the verdict and the death sentence with startling calm.
bg: Plato was present at the trial, though the Apology is a literary work rather than a transcript. Apology here means a formal defence, not an apology in the modern sense. It is one of the earliest portraits of Socrates and among the most widely read works of ancient philosophy.
br: Very short: read it in one sitting, ideally aloud. It is a speech, and its irony, its jokes and its sudden seriousness work best when heard. Notice when the tone shifts after the verdict.
la: Socrates claims to be a plain speaker while dismantling his accusers by cross-examination, so the reader sees the very method he is on trial for practised in the courtroom. His refusal to flatter the jury is both principled and provocative.
cx: Athens had recently endured military defeat, a brutal pro-Spartan oligarchy and civil strife, and some of Socrates’ former associates were linked to that regime. That history helps explain the hostility toward him that the speech never mentions directly.
th: Wisdom and ignorance
Knowing that you do not know is the beginning of wisdom.
Conscience and law
Faithfulness to one’s calling can outrank the commands of the city.
Death without fear
No one knows whether death is an evil, so fearing it is a false claim to knowledge.
fit: The quickest route to understanding why Socrates matters; a perfect companion to the Republic and the Symposium.
mis: To some readers Socrates seems arrogant and self-sabotaging rather than heroic. Its brevity also leaves many questions open.
rq: Is Socrates actually trying to win?
What does the unexamined life mean in practice?
Why does he propose free meals for life as his penalty?
dq: Was Athens right by its own laws?
Does conscience ever justify defying a democratic majority?
rel: Another face of Socrates, at a party rather than a trial.

sum: Nietzsche’s most joyful book gathers hundreds of aphorisms on art, science, love, morality and the meaning of life once belief in God has faded. It contains the famous parable of the madman who runs into the marketplace announcing that God is dead, and the first statement of eternal recurrence: the challenge to live so that you would will your life to repeat forever.
bg: First published in 1882 and expanded in 1887 with a new preface, a fifth book and an appendix of songs, The Gay Science (Die fröhliche Wissenschaft) comes from Nietzsche’s middle period, just before Thus Spoke Zarathustra, which it introduces in its final section.
br: Dip in rather than racing through; aphorisms reward rereading and argument. Gay here means joyful: the title echoes the Provençal troubadours’ name for the art of poetry. Book Five, added later, is the most reflective.
la: Nietzsche writes in fragments, jokes, poems and provocations that refuse to build a system, asking readers to test each idea against their own lives rather than accept a doctrine.
cx: The book was written during years of illness and wandering after Nietzsche left his professorship in Basel. It reflects his break with Wagner and with Schopenhauer’s pessimism, and his search for a way to say yes to life without religious guarantees.
th: The death of God
Once old foundations fail, every value has to be rethought.
Affirmation
Could you embrace your life so fully that you would live it again forever?
Knowledge as adventure
Inquiry can be cheerful, daring and experimental rather than grim.
fit: A livelier entry to Nietzsche than his polemics, and a link to the existentialist titles on your plan.
mis: The fragmentary form can feel scattered, and individual lines are easily misread out of context.
cw: Some passages contain dated or hostile views on women.
rq: What exactly has died when God is dead?
How would you answer the demon of eternal recurrence?
Which aphorism do you disagree with most strongly?
dq: How does humour serve his philosophy?
rel: Camus’ answer to the same loss of meaning.

g: Philosophy; critique of morality and metaphysics
sum: Nietzsche accuses philosophers of passing off their personal prejudices as universal truths, and calls for free spirits who can think beyond conventional ideas of good and evil. Across nine parts he examines religion, morality, scholarship, nationalism, and the will to power, ending with a sketch of what a higher, nobler humanity might look like.
bg: Published at Nietzsche’s own expense in 1886, it was meant to restate the ideas of Thus Spoke Zarathustra in plainer prose. It is often recommended as the best single overview of his mature thought, and its subtitle calls it a prelude to a philosophy of the future.
br: The preface and first part set out the agenda; read slowly and argue back in the margins. A translation with notes, such as Kaufmann’s or the Cambridge edition, will clarify his many targets.
la: Nietzsche writes as a psychologist of ideas, asking what drives a belief and whom it serves rather than only whether it is true. Short numbered sections alternate between sustained argument and biting epigram.
cx: He writes against Kant, Christianity and the democratic and nationalist movements of nineteenth-century Europe. His later misappropriation by fascists, helped by his sister’s editing of his papers, distorted views he held, including his contempt for antisemitism.
th: Perspectivism
Every philosophy expresses a particular perspective and set of needs.
Master and slave morality
Moral values have a history and a psychology behind them.
The free spirit
Thinking for yourself demands discomfort, solitude and a kind of courage.
fit: A rigorous counterweight to Kant’s Groundwork, Mill’s Utilitarianism and On Liberty already in your plan.
mis: Its aristocratic tone and some openly sexist passages can alienate readers, and the style is deliberately provocative.
rq: What prejudice does Nietzsche find hidden in philosophers?
What would living beyond good and evil look like day to day?
Which of his diagnoses still fits our world?
dq: Is Nietzsche a moralist after all?

g: Philosophy; three essays on the history of moral values
sum: In three linked essays Nietzsche traces how our ideas of good and evil, of guilt, bad conscience and duty, and of ascetic self-denial came into being. He argues that much of modern morality grew not from reason or revelation but from resentment, debt and cruelty turned inward, and asks what that history means for whether we should keep these values.
bg: Written in 1887 as a sequel and clarification of Beyond Good and Evil, the Genealogy is Nietzsche’s most structured work and a cornerstone of modern moral philosophy, influencing Freud, Foucault and much twentieth-century critical theory. It is the work most often taught in university courses on Nietzsche.
br: Read one essay at a time. The first, on good and bad versus good and evil, is the most famous; the second, on guilt and debt, is often the most rewarding and disturbing.
la: Nietzsche’s genealogical method treats values as historical products rather than timeless truths. He combines philology, speculative history, psychology and polemic, and expects readers to ruminate rather than skim.
cx: The book’s imagery of nobles and slaves, and some of its remarks about Jews, were later abused by antisemites whom Nietzsche himself despised. Reading with a good introduction helps separate his argument from that history.
th: Ressentiment
The powerless revalue strength as evil and weakness as virtue.
Guilt and debt
Conscience grew out of punishment, promise-keeping and obligation.
Ascetic ideals
Even self-denial can be a hidden expression of the will to power.
fit: The best place to see Nietzsche argue at length, sharpening your reading of Kant, Mill and Aristotle.
mis: Its historical claims are speculative, and the rhetoric of masters and slaves can repel.
cw: Graphic discussion of punishment and cruelty.
Antisemitic tropes that Nietzsche critiques but sometimes echoes.
rq: How do good and bad differ from good and evil?
Why does Nietzsche link guilt to debt?
What do ascetic ideals give the people who hold them?
dq: Does knowing where a value came from discredit it?
What might a morality without ressentiment look like?
rel: The book this sequel clarifies and extends.
